item.title: Stack test
item.dc:creator: Nam Le
item.description:
Consider a flow generated by

Definition 1 (Hyperbolic fixed point) A point is hyperbolic if has no eigenvalues on the imaginary axis.

Theorem 1 (Hartman–Grobman) Near a hyperbolic fixed point (Definition 1), the flow of Equation 1 is topologically conjugate to its linearization (Strogatz 2015).

Proof. Omitted.

Figure 1 shows the damped pendulum .

Code 
import numpy as np
import matplotlib.pyplot as plt

th, om = np.meshgrid(np.linspace(-2*np.pi, 2*np.pi, 40), np.linspace(-3, 3, 30))

# One figure per theme; Quarto shows the one matching the reader's light/dark mode.
for fg, line in [("#212529", "#2c5f9e"), ("#dee2e6", "#8ab8f0")]:
    with plt.rc_context({"text.color": fg, "axes.labelcolor": fg, "axes.edgecolor": fg,
                         "xtick.color": fg, "ytick.color": fg,
                         "figure.facecolor": "none", "axes.facecolor": "none"}):
        fig, ax = plt.subplots(figsize=(7, 3.5))
        ax.streamplot(th, om, om, -np.sin(th) - 0.3*om, density=1.2, linewidth=0.7, color=line)
        ax.set_xlabel(r"$\theta$")
        ax.set_ylabel(r"$\dot\theta$")
        plt.show()

Interactive: vary the damping

Drag the slider to change in . The trajectories are computed in your browser, so nothing here depends on the frozen Python output. At the orbits around the origin close up; any turns them into spirals.

Code 
viewof c = Inputs.range([0, 1], {value: 0.3, step: 0.01, label: "Damping c"})
Code 
// Integrate a grid of initial conditions with RK4.
trajectories = {
  const f = ([th, om]) => [om, -Math.sin(th) - c * om];
  const step = (x, h) => {
    const k1 = f(x);
    const k2 = f([x[0] + h/2 * k1[0], x[1] + h/2 * k1[1]]);
    const k3 = f([x[0] + h/2 * k2[0], x[1] + h/2 * k2[1]]);
    const k4 = f([x[0] + h * k3[0], x[1] + h * k3[1]]);
    return [x[0] + h/6 * (k1[0] + 2*k2[0] + 2*k3[0] + k4[0]),
            x[1] + h/6 * (k1[1] + 2*k2[1] + 2*k3[1] + k4[1])];
  };
  const starts = [];
  for (let th0 = -2 * Math.PI; th0 <= 2 * Math.PI + 1e-9; th0 += Math.PI / 3)
    for (const om0 of [-2.8, -1.2, 1.2, 2.8]) starts.push([th0, om0]);
  return starts.flatMap((x0, id) => {
    let x = x0;
    const pts = [{id, th: x[0], om: x[1]}];
    for (let i = 0; i < 800 && Math.abs(x[0]) < 2 * Math.PI + 1 && Math.abs(x[1]) < 4; i++) {
      x = step(x, 0.025);
      pts.push({id, th: x[0], om: x[1]});
    }
    return pts;
  });
}
Code 
Plot.plot({
  className: "phase-plot",
  width,
  height: 340,
  x: {domain: [-2 * Math.PI, 2 * Math.PI], label: "θ"},
  y: {domain: [-3, 3], label: "θ̇"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line(trajectories, {x: "th", y: "om", z: "id", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 1.1, strokeOpacity: 0.8, clip: true}),
    Plot.dot([-2, -1, 0, 1, 2].map(k => ({th: k * Math.PI, saddle: k % 2 !== 0})),
             {x: "th", y: () => 0, r: 4, fill: d => d.saddle ? "none" : "currentColor", stroke: "currentColor"})
  ]
})

References

Strogatz, Steven H. 2015. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos. 2nd ed. Westview Press.

item.title: The Lorenz system
item.dc:creator: Nam Le
item.description:
The Poincaré–Bendixson theorem rules out chaos for planar flows. Lorenz (1963) found it in three dimensions, in a drastically truncated model of convection: Lorenz’s parameters, used throughout, are , and .

Basic structure

Three properties can be read off Equation 1 directly.

  • Symmetry. The equations are unchanged by , so every trajectory has a mirror twin.
  • Dissipation. The divergence of the vector field is , a constant. By Liouville’s theorem, volumes in phase space shrink like , so the attractor has zero volume.
  • Equilibria. The origin is always an equilibrium. For there are two more,

Proposition 1 For every trajectory of Equation 1 tends to the origin.

Proof. Take . A direct computation gives For we have , so away from the origin. Since is radially unbounded, the origin is globally asymptotically stable by the Lyapunov and LaSalle theorems.

As increases, appear at and are stable until a subcritical Hopf bifurcation at At all three equilibria are unstable. Yet trajectories stay bounded, since every one eventually enters a fixed large ellipsoid (Strogatz 2015, sec. 9.2). Combined with the dissipation above, they wander forever on a bounded set of zero volume without settling down.

The attractor

Code 
sigma, beta, rho = 10.0, 8 / 3, 28.0
lorenz = lambda u: np.array([sigma * (u[1] - u[0]), u[0] * (rho - u[2]) - u[1], u[0] * u[1] - beta * u[2]])
t, u = rk4(lorenz, [1.0, 1.0, 1.0], 60, h=0.005)
u = u[t > 5]
c_eq = np.sqrt(beta * (rho - 1))

def draw(fig, ax, c):
    ax.plot(u[:, 0], u[:, 2], color=c.accent, lw=0.35, alpha=0.9)
    ax.plot([c_eq, -c_eq], [rho - 1, rho - 1], "o", color=c.accent2, ms=5)
    ax.set(xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel=r"$z$")

themed(draw, figsize=(7, 5))

The trajectory circles one equilibrium, then the other, switching in a sequence that looks random. Whether this picture really contains a strange attractor, rather than being a numerical artifact, stayed open until Tucker (2002) settled it with a computer-assisted proof.

Sensitive dependence

Figure 2 follows two trajectories that start apart on the attractor. Their distance grows roughly like , where is the largest Lyapunov exponent of the attractor, until it reaches the size of the attractor itself. After that the two trajectories are unrelated. This is why weather forecasts have a horizon, however good the model.

Code 
start = u[-1]  # a point already on the attractor, from the previous figure
t, a = rk4(lorenz, start, 45, h=0.005)
_, b = rk4(lorenz, start + [1e-8, 0, 0], 45, h=0.005)
dist = np.linalg.norm(a - b, axis=1)

def draw(fig, ax, c):
    ax.semilogy(t, dist, color=c.accent, lw=1)
    ax.semilogy(t, 1e-8 * np.exp(0.906 * t), "--", color=c.accent2, lw=1, label=r"$10^{-8} e^{0.906\,t}$")
    ax.set(xlabel=r"$t$", ylabel="distance", ylim=(1e-9, 1e3))
    ax.legend(loc="lower right")

themed(draw, figsize=(7, 3.6))

For more on the Lorenz equations, see Strogatz (2015, ch. 9) and Hirsch et al. (2013, ch. 14).

References

Hirsch, Morris W., Stephen Smale, and Robert L. Devaney. 2013. Differential Equations, Dynamical Systems, and an Introduction to Chaos. 3rd ed. Academic Press.
Lorenz, Edward N. 1963. “Deterministic Nonperiodic Flow.” Journal of the Atmospheric Sciences 20 (2): 130–41.
Strogatz, Steven H. 2015. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos. 2nd ed. Westview Press.
Tucker, Warwick. 2002. “A Rigorous ODE Solver and Smale’s 14th Problem.” Foundations of Computational Mathematics 2 (1): 53–117.

item.title: Lyapunov exponents of one-dimensional maps
item.dc:creator: Nam Le
item.description:
The bifurcation diagram of the logistic map shows where orbits stop being periodic, but not how chaotic they are. The Lyapunov exponent measures this as the average exponential rate at which nearby orbits separate.

Definition

Two orbits of a map that start apart are, to first order, apart after steps, by the chain rule. Taking logarithms and averaging gives the following.

Definition 1 (Lyapunov exponent) The Lyapunov exponent of the orbit of under a map is when the limit exists.

A negative means nearby orbits converge, as they do onto a stable periodic orbit. A positive means they separate exponentially, which is sensitive dependence on initial conditions. At a period-doubling point the multiplier is , so there.

Proposition 1 If lies on a periodic orbit of period , then . In particular for a stable cycle with multiplier of modulus less than 1.

Proof. The sum in Equation 1 repeats with period , and by the chain rule .

Computing it

For the logistic map we have . The code below discards a transient, then averages over 2000 iterations for each of 3000 values of .

Code 
r = np.linspace(2.8, 4.0, 3000)
x = np.full_like(r, 0.3)
for _ in range(1000):
    x = r * x * (1 - x)
lam = np.zeros_like(r)
n = 2000
for _ in range(n):
    x = r * x * (1 - x)
    lam += np.log(np.maximum(np.abs(r * (1 - 2 * x)), 1e-12))
lam /= n

def draw(fig, ax, c):
    ax.axhline(0, color=c.muted, lw=0.8)
    ax.axhline(np.log(2), color=c.accent2, lw=0.8, ls="--")
    ax.text(2.82, np.log(2) + 0.06, r"$\ln 2$", color=c.accent2)
    ax.plot(r, lam, color=c.accent, lw=0.6)
    ax.set(xlim=(2.8, 4), ylim=(-2, 1), xlabel=r"$r$", ylabel=r"$\lambda$")

themed(draw, figsize=(8, 3.8))

At the average settles very close to :

Code 
x, total, n = 0.3, 0.0, 200_000
for _ in range(n):
    x = 4 * x * (1 - x)
    total += np.log(abs(4 * (1 - 2 * x)))
print(f"lambda(4) ≈ {total / n:.4f},  ln 2 = {np.log(2):.4f}")
lambda(4) ≈ 0.6931,  ln 2 = 0.6931

Why exactly at

Proposition 2 Let be the tent map on and . Then .

Proof. . For , . For , .

So the logistic map at is the tent map in disguise. The tent map stretches every interval by exactly a factor of 2, so its exponent is for every orbit that avoids the kink at . The change of variables is smooth with a smooth inverse on the open interval, and this does not change the long-run average for typical orbits, so for Lebesgue-almost every (Strogatz 2015, sec. 10.5).

Remark. Floating-point arithmetic cannot follow an individual chaotic orbit for long: with , the rounding error doubles each step and swamps the orbit after about 50 iterations. The computed average is still meaningful in practice: the rounded sequence behaves statistically like a typical true orbit, and averages like Equation 1 are the same for almost every true orbit. Shadowing theorems make this kind of argument rigorous for some classes of systems.

References

Strogatz, Steven H. 2015. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos. 2nd ed. Westview Press.

item.title: The logistic map and period doubling
item.dc:creator: Nam Le
item.description:
May (1976) argued that even the simplest nonlinear models deserve careful study, because their behavior can be astonishingly rich. The standard example is the logistic map

Fixed points and the first doubling

Proposition 1 For , the fixed point of Equation 1 is stable, and it loses stability at .

Proof. A fixed point of a map is stable when . Here , so , and exactly when .

At the multiplier passes through . Orbits near then alternate from side to side, and a stable orbit of period 2 appears.

Proposition 2 The period-2 orbit of Equation 1 exists for and is stable for .

Proof. The points are the roots of other than the fixed points, namely the roots of . These are real and distinct exactly when . They satisfy and . The multiplier of the cycle is This equals at and at , and lies strictly between them for .

Try it: cobweb diagram

A cobweb diagram iterates the map graphically: go up to the curve, across to the diagonal, and repeat. Try (spiralling into the fixed point), (a 2-cycle), (a 4-cycle) and (chaos).

Code 
viewof r = Inputs.range([2.5, 4], {value: 3.2, step: 0.001, label: "r"})
viewof x0 = Inputs.range([0.01, 0.99], {value: 0.2, step: 0.01, label: "x₀"})
Code 
cobweb = {
  const f = (x) => r * x * (1 - x);
  const pts = [{x: x0, y: 0}];
  let x = x0;
  for (let i = 0; i < 80; i++) {
    const y = f(x);
    pts.push({x, y}, {x: y, y});
    x = y;
  }
  return pts;
}
curve = d3.range(0, 1.0001, 0.005).map((x) => ({x, y: r * x * (1 - x)}))
Code 
Plot.plot({
  className: "phase-plot",
  width: Math.min(width, 560),
  height: Math.min(width, 560),
  x: {domain: [0, 1], label: "xₙ"},
  y: {domain: [0, 1], label: "xₙ₊₁"},
  marks: [
    Plot.line([{x: 0, y: 0}, {x: 1, y: 1}], {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "currentColor", strokeOpacity: 0.4}),
    Plot.line(curve, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 2}),
    Plot.line(cobweb, {x: "x", y: "y", stroke: "currentColor", strokeWidth: 0.9, strokeOpacity: 0.75})
  ]
})

The cascade

The 2-cycle itself doubles to a 4-cycle, then an 8-cycle, and so on. The doublings accumulate at , beyond which most parameter values give chaotic orbits (Figure 1). The chaotic region is broken by periodic windows. The widest begins at with a stable 3-cycle.

Code 
r = np.linspace(2.5, 4.0, 2000)
x = np.full_like(r, 0.5)
for _ in range(1000):
    x = r * x * (1 - x)
R, Xs = [], []
for _ in range(250):
    x = r * x * (1 - x)
    R.append(r)
    Xs.append(x)
R, Xs = np.concatenate(R), np.concatenate(Xs)

def draw(fig, ax, c):
    ax.scatter(R, Xs, s=0.05, lw=0, color=c.accent, alpha=0.5, rasterized=True)
    for rv in (3, 1 + np.sqrt(6), 1 + np.sqrt(8)):
        ax.axvline(rv, color=c.muted, lw=0.6, ls=":")
    ax.set(xlim=(2.5, 4), ylim=(0, 1), xlabel=r"$r$", ylabel=r"$x$")

themed(draw, figsize=(8, 4.2))

If is the parameter of the -th doubling, the ratios of successive gaps converge: Feigenbaum (1978) discovered that this constant is universal: the same appears for any smooth one-humped map with a quadratic maximum, and it has since been measured in fluid, electronic and chemical experiments. The next post makes “chaotic” precise with Lyapunov exponents.

References

Feigenbaum, Mitchell J. 1978. “Quantitative Universality for a Class of Nonlinear Transformations.” Journal of Statistical Physics 19 (1): 25–52. https://doi.org/10.1007/BF01020332.
May, Robert M. 1976. “Simple Mathematical Models with Very Complicated Dynamics.” Nature 261: 459–67. https://doi.org/10.1038/261459a0.

item.title: The Hopf bifurcation
item.dc:creator: Nam Le
item.description:
In the trace–determinant plane, a stable spiral becomes unstable by crossing the line , where a pair of complex eigenvalues passes through the imaginary axis. The linear system has no way to describe what happens next. The nonlinear system typically gains or loses a periodic orbit.

The normal form

Example 1 In polar coordinates, consider For , for all , and the origin is a stable spiral. For the origin is an unstable spiral, and the circle is a stable limit cycle, since inside it and outside it.

The cycle is born at zero amplitude and grows like (Figure 1), while its period stays close to . Replacing by gives the subcritical case: an unstable cycle shrinks onto the origin as , and past the bifurcation trajectories jump away to some distant attractor.

Code 
mu_neg, mu_pos = np.linspace(-1, 0, 50), np.linspace(0, 1, 200)

def draw(fig, ax, c):
    ax.plot(mu_neg, 0 * mu_neg, color=c.accent, lw=2, label="stable")
    ax.plot(mu_pos, 0 * mu_pos, "--", color=c.accent2, lw=2, label="unstable")
    ax.plot(mu_pos, np.sqrt(mu_pos), color=c.accent, lw=2)
    ax.text(0.2, 0.85, r"limit cycle $r = \sqrt{\mu}$", ha="center")
    ax.set(xlabel=r"$\mu$", ylabel=r"amplitude $r$", ylim=(-0.1, 1.2))
    ax.legend(loc="upper left")

themed(draw, figsize=(7, 3.4))

The general theorem

Any planar system at such a crossing behaves like Equation 1, provided two nondegeneracy conditions hold.

Theorem 1 (Hopf bifurcation in the plane) Let be a smooth family on with an equilibrium whose linearization has eigenvalues . Suppose

  1. and ;
  2. (the eigenvalues cross the imaginary axis with nonzero speed);
  3. the first Lyapunov coefficient , computed from the second and third derivatives of at , is nonzero.

Then for near on one side of the bifurcation there is a unique periodic orbit near , with amplitude of order and period close to . If the bifurcation is supercritical and the orbit is stable; if it is subcritical and the orbit is unstable.

See Guckenheimer and Holmes (1983, sec. 3.4) for the formula for and the proof, which reduces the system to Equation 1 by a near-identity change of coordinates.

Example: the Brusselator

Example 2 The Brusselator is a model of an oscillating chemical reaction: Its only equilibrium is , with Jacobian So changes sign at . The eigenvalues there are , and , so conditions 1 and 2 of Theorem 1 hold with .

Figure 2 takes , so . Below trajectories spiral into the equilibrium. Above it the equilibrium repels, and trajectories from inside and outside settle onto a stable limit cycle, consistent with a supercritical bifurcation.

Code 
a = 1.0

def brusselator(b):
    return lambda x: np.array([a - (b + 1) * x[0] + x[0]**2 * x[1], b * x[0] - x[0]**2 * x[1]])

_, below = rk4(brusselator(1.8), [2.0, 1.0], 60, h=0.01)
_, above_in = rk4(brusselator(2.5), [1.05, 2.5], 40, h=0.01)
_, above_out = rk4(brusselator(2.5), [0.3, 4.2], 40, h=0.01)

def draw(fig, axes, c):
    for ax, b, paths in ((axes[0], 1.8, [below]), (axes[1], 2.5, [above_in, above_out])):
        for p, col in zip(paths, (c.accent, c.accent2)):
            ax.plot(p[:, 0], p[:, 1], color=col, lw=1.1)
        ax.plot(a, b / a, "o", color=c.fg, ms=5)
        ax.set(title=fr"$b = {b}$", xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel=r"$y$")

themed(draw, 1, 2, figsize=(8, 3.8))

References

Guckenheimer, John, and Philip Holmes. 1983. Nonlinear Oscillations, Dynamical Systems, and Bifurcations of Vector Fields. Vol. 42. Applied Mathematical Sciences. Springer.

item.title: The Poincaré–Bendixson theorem
item.dc:creator: Nam Le
item.description:
Equilibria are found by solving . Periodic orbits are much harder to find, since they are global objects. In the plane there is a clean topological criterion for their existence.

Theorem 1 (Poincaré–Bendixson) Let be on an open set containing a closed bounded region , and suppose contains no equilibria of . If some trajectory starts in and stays in for all , then it is a closed orbit or it spirals toward a closed orbit as . In either case contains a closed orbit.

The proof rests on the Jordan curve theorem: a closed curve splits the plane into an inside and an outside, so a planar trajectory cannot weave around itself the way it can in three dimensions (Perko 2001, sec. 3.7). In practice the theorem is applied through trapping regions.

Corollary 1 (Trapping regions) Let be a closed annulus containing no equilibria. If the vector field points into everywhere on its boundary, then contains a closed orbit.

Proof. Any trajectory starting in can never leave it, so Theorem 1 applies.

A worked example

Example 1 Following Strogatz (2015, sec. 7.3), consider in polar coordinates with . There are no equilibria except the origin, since . On a circle with , so and the flow points outward. On a circle with , the same bound in the other direction gives . The annulus is therefore a trapping region, and by Corollary 1 it contains a closed orbit.

Figure 1 shows the result for : trajectories from inside and outside are drawn to a single closed orbit lying between the circles and .

Code 
mu = 0.5

def field(x):
    r = np.hypot(x[0], x[1])
    g = 1 - r**2 + (mu * x[0] / r if r > 0 else 0.0)
    return np.array([x[0] * g - x[1], x[1] * g + x[0]])

g = np.linspace(-1.8, 1.8, 40)
X, Y = np.meshgrid(g, g)
R = np.hypot(X, Y)
G = 1 - R**2 + mu * np.divide(X, R, out=np.zeros_like(X), where=R > 0)
U, W = X * G - Y, Y * G + X

_, inner = rk4(field, [0.15, 0.0], 12, h=0.01)
_, outer = rk4(field, [1.75, 0.0], 12, h=0.01)
_, cycle = rk4(field, inner[-1], 2 * np.pi, h=0.01)
phi = np.linspace(0, 2 * np.pi, 200)

def draw(fig, ax, c):
    ax.streamplot(X, Y, U, W, color=c.muted, density=0.8, linewidth=0.5, arrowsize=0.7)
    for rad in (np.sqrt(1 - mu), np.sqrt(1 + mu)):
        ax.plot(rad * np.cos(phi), rad * np.sin(phi), "--", color=c.fg, lw=1)
    ax.plot(inner[:, 0], inner[:, 1], color=c.accent2, lw=1)
    ax.plot(outer[:, 0], outer[:, 1], color=c.accent2, lw=1)
    ax.plot(cycle[:, 0], cycle[:, 1], color=c.accent, lw=2.2)
    ax.set(xlim=(-1.8, 1.8), ylim=(-1.8, 1.8), aspect="equal", xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel=r"$y$")

themed(draw, figsize=(5.5, 5.5))

The van der Pol oscillator

The same idea, with a more careful choice of region, proves that the van der Pol oscillator has a periodic orbit. Liénard’s theorem goes further and shows the orbit is unique and attracts every trajectory except the equilibrium at the origin (Perko 2001, sec. 3.8). Figure 2 shows how the cycle changes shape: nearly circular for small , and a relaxation oscillation with slow drifts and fast jumps for large .

Code 
def vdp(mu):
    f = lambda x: np.array([x[1], mu * (1 - x[0]**2) * x[1] - x[0]])
    _, xs = rk4(f, [0.5, 0.0], 60, h=0.005)
    return xs[len(xs) // 2:]

cycles = {m: vdp(m) for m in (0.3, 1.0, 3.0)}

def draw(fig, ax, c):
    for (m, xs), col in zip(cycles.items(), (c.accent, c.accent2, c.fg)):
        ax.plot(xs[:, 0], xs[:, 1], color=col, lw=1.4, label=fr"$\mu = {m:g}$")
    ax.set(xlabel=r"$x$", ylabel=r"$\dot x$")
    ax.legend(loc="upper left")

themed(draw, figsize=(7, 4.2))

Remark. Theorem 1 is also the reason chaos needs at least three dimensions: in the plane, a bounded trajectory away from equilibria can only settle onto a closed orbit. The Lorenz system escapes this by living in .

References

Perko, Lawrence. 2001. Differential Equations and Dynamical Systems. 3rd ed. Springer.
Strogatz, Steven H. 2015. Nonlinear Dynamics and Chaos. 2nd ed. Westview Press.

item.title: Lyapunov functions and LaSalle’s principle
item.dc:creator: Nam Le
item.description:
Linearization decides stability only at hyperbolic equilibria. Lyapunov’s second method works directly with the nonlinear system by finding a quantity that decreases along solutions, the way energy does in a mechanical system with friction.

Stability and Lyapunov functions

Definition 1 (Stability) The equilibrium of Equation 1 is stable if for every there is such that implies for all . It is asymptotically stable if in addition for all close enough to .

Theorem 1 (Lyapunov) If has a Lyapunov function, it is stable. If moreover for all , it is asymptotically stable.

A solution starting there has for all , so it can never reach the sphere. For the strict case, decreases to some limit . When is only semi-definite

The natural Lyapunov function is often the energy, and friction usually removes energy only when something is moving. That gives but not , and Theorem 1 stops at plain stability. LaSalle’s invariance principle closes the gap (LaSalle 1960).

Theorem 2 (LaSalle’s invariance principle) Let be a compact set that is positively invariant for Equation 1, and let be with on . Let be the largest invariant set contained in . Then every solution starting in approaches as .

Example 2 (The damped pendulum) Take with , written as , . The energy satisfies . It vanishes on the whole line , so Theorem 1 only gives stability.

For the sublevel set is compact and positively invariant, and . A solution that stays in has , so and . So , and by Theorem 2 the bottom equilibrium is asymptotically stable.

Figure 1 shows this: the trajectory crosses the level sets of inward, and decreases in steps, pausing each time the pendulum turns around ().

Hyperbolicity

The classification also says when linearization can be trusted. An equilibrium is hyperbolic when no eigenvalue has zero real part, and the Hartman–Grobman theorem says that near a hyperbolic equilibrium a nonlinear flow looks like its linearization.
